cards.title: pytest.mark.parametrize for Test Cases
cards.teaser: `@pytest.mark.parametrize` runs the same test function multiple times with different inputs. Each combination becomes a separate, independently reported test case — so one failure doesn't hide others, and the test ID tells you exactly which input broke.

Combine parametrize with fixtures: a parametrized test can still declare fixtures as parameters; pytest handles the injection for each case independently.

runs.text: Keep parametrized data close to the test — a list of tuples defined just above the decorator. For very large datasets, load from a fixture that reads a JSON or CSV file, keeping the test readable and the data maintainable.

Parametrize is a for-loop turned into a test decorator. You give it a list of inputs and expected outputs, and it runs your test once for each row — each run reported and tracked separately, so one broken case can't hide the others.

runs.text: Over-mocking is a test smell. If every collaborator in a test is mocked, you're testing the mock configuration, not the code. Mock at the boundary of your system (HTTP client, database driver) rather than every internal helper.

A Mock is a recording double that says 'yes' to anything. patch swaps a real thing for a Mock during the test and puts the original back when done. You use patch to stop real HTTP calls or database writes from happening, then check the Mock's diary to confirm the right calls were made.

cards.title: Property-Based Testing with Hypothesis
cards.teaser: `hypothesis` generates hundreds of random inputs that satisfy your declared constraints and checks whether your function's invariants hold for all of them. When it finds a failure it shrinks the input to the smallest reproducing example and shows you exactly what broke.

runs.text: Traditional tests check specific examples you thought of. Property-based testing with
valid inputs. For a sort function the invariant might be: the output is the same length as the input and each adjacent pair satisfies

and Hypothesis calls your test function with hundreds of generated lists.

items.text: Hypothesis caches failing examples in a
database — it always replays known-failing inputs on the next run, so regressions aren't hidden by random sampling.

runs.text: Hypothesis excels at finding edge cases you didn't think of: empty collections, integers at
, NaN floats, strings with Unicode surrogates, empty strings. These are exactly the inputs that cause production bugs.

Instead of picking a few specific examples, you tell Hypothesis what kinds of inputs are valid and what should always be true about your output. It then throws hundreds of random inputs at your code to find a case where your 'always true' claim breaks — and if it finds one, it shows you the smallest possible example.

cards.title: Doctest for Executable Examples
cards.teaser: `doctest` extracts Python interactive-session examples from docstrings and runs them as tests. The examples double as documentation and are automatically verified — if the code changes but the docstring doesn't, the test fails.

runs.text: A doctest is a snippet in a docstring that looks like a Python REPL session: lines starting with
are executed, and the expected output is the text on the following lines. The
module finds these snippets, runs them, and compares actual output to expected output. The test fails if they differ.
. The integration is valuable: doctests live in the same file as the code, stay close to the function they describe, and get run automatically in CI alongside the rest of the test suite.

runs.text: Use doctest for short, illustrative examples in public APIs — the kind of 'here's how you call this' snippet that belongs in documentation. Use pytest for thorough behavioral testing. The two are complementary, not competing.

A doctest is a copy-paste of a Python shell session inside your docstring. Python runs those lines and checks that the output matches what you wrote. Your documentation becomes executable — if the code changes and the example is now wrong, the test fails.

cards.title: Integration vs Unit Test Tradeoffs
cards.teaser: Unit tests isolate one function with all collaborators mocked — fast, precise, fragile to refactors. Integration tests wire several components together against real dependencies — slower, but they catch contract mismatches that unit tests miss. Both belong in a healthy test suite.

runs.text: tests one logical unit — typically a single function or class — with its external dependencies replaced by mocks or stubs. Unit tests run in milliseconds, give precise failure signals, and are easy to maintain. Their weakness: they test each piece in isolation, so a bug at the boundary between two correctly-tested units goes undetected.

connects real components: a service against a real database, an HTTP client against a test server, multiple modules wired together. Integration tests catch contract mismatches, serialization bugs, and configuration errors that unit tests miss. The cost: slower execution, harder setup, and failures that can be harder to isolate.

items.text: : many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle, very few end-to-end tests at the top. Invert this pyramid and CI becomes painfully slow.
Unit tests are more valuable for pure business logic (algorithms, validations, transformations). Integration tests are more valuable for I/O-heavy code (database queries, API calls, file parsing).

runs.text: The right split depends on your domain. A data-pipeline service benefits heavily from integration tests against real filesystems and databases. A pure-computation library benefits from exhaustive unit tests and Hypothesis property tests.

Unit tests check that each brick is solid in isolation. Integration tests check that the bricks fit together and the structure stands. You need both — a wall of perfect bricks still fails if the mortar is wrong. The art is knowing how many of each to write.

cards.title: Test Doubles: Mocks vs Stubs vs Fakes
cards.teaser: A stub returns a canned answer; a mock records calls and asserts on them; a fake is a working but lightweight implementation. Knowing which to use prevents over-mocking — the test smells where every collaborator is a Mock and tests verify call patterns instead of behavior.

items.text: Prefer fakes for complex dependencies — a fake repository backed by a dict is more realistic than a Mock and simpler than a real database. Fakes tend to produce tests that survive refactors better.

runs.text: The key question when choosing a test double: 'Am I testing that the right

A stub is a cardboard cutout that hands back a scripted answer. A mock is a spy that also checks you asked the right questions. A fake is a lightweight working replacement — like an in-memory database. Use the simplest double that lets your test make the assertion it needs.

cards.title: Debugging Strategies
cards.teaser: Print debugging is fast for simple bugs; structured logging captures context in production; bisecting a history of changes isolates when a bug was introduced; and systematic hypothesis-and-test thinking beats random code thrashing every time.

runs.text: Debugging is a skill, not just a toolset. The most effective strategy is the

: form a hypothesis about what is wrong, make the smallest possible change to test it, observe the result, and revise. Randomly changing code and re-running rarely finds the root cause — it produces more variables and more confusion.

Reproduce first, fix second. If you can't reliably reproduce a bug, you can't verify the fix. Write a failing test that demonstrates the bug before touching production code.

runs.text: The best debugging session is one you avoid by writing tests first. A failing test that reproduces a bug is both a diagnosis tool and a regression guard — once you fix the bug and the test passes, you know the fix is correct and it can never silently regress.

Debugging is really just applying the scientific method to broken code. Form a hypothesis, run the smallest experiment that could prove it wrong, observe the result. The tools — print, logging, pdb, git bisect — are just ways to run faster experiments. The thinking is what matters.
